title: Response-Style Simulator
summary: Seven fictional respondents with the same true standing answer the same twenty items very differently. Compare the grids, then work out what a response pattern can and cannot tell you.
learningObjectives: Recognise acquiescent, extreme, midpoint, impression-managed, random, straight-lined and attentive response patterns from their evidence.
Explain why balanced keying neutralises acquiescence and why an unbalanced scale cannot distinguish it from a high score.
Explain why a total score reflects how a person uses a rating scale as well as the trait.
State what a response pattern can establish and what it cannot.
Frame a data-screening decision as a stated methodological choice rather than a judgement about respondents.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Every answer is printed as its own digit inside its cell, so a response grid is readable as text and the shading is a redundant cue rather than the carrier. Reverse-keyed items are marked with a dotted underline and described in the text, never by colour alone. The distribution chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible summary table. Native checkboxes, radios, range and number inputs throughout; sliders announce meaningful values. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Response styles: what a rating pattern shows, why balanced keying matters, and what no pattern can establish about a motive
simulationNotes: Seven fictional respondents sharing one true standing on an unnamed trait, answering twenty generated items on a 1-5 scale. Each style is a transformation of the same underlying response. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator with the seed shown and settable. No real questionnaire, item or dataset is reproduced. Styles are modelled as pure and constant, which real respondents are not; detection uses five simple summary statistics rather than long-string indices, person-fit statistics or response latencies. Impression management is modelled as a shift towards the desirable end and is explicitly not a measure of deception. The tool never attributes a motive to a pattern and marks any answer that does as overreaching.
